/ai/foundations/what-is-an-llm.def: A large language model (LLM) is a program trained on a huge amount of text to predict the next token (a small piece of a word). By predicting one token after another, it writes answers, summaries and code.
/ai/foundations/what-is-an-llm.why: Writing rules by hand for every language task is impossible. Training one model on a huge amount of text gives a single tool that can handle many tasks from plain instructions. The price is that it produces likely text, not checked facts.
use: You need to understand, write, summarise, translate or classify text
You can describe the task in plain language or with a few examples
A mistake can be caught by a person or a check
avoid: You need exact, always-correct answers (calculations, lookups in a database)
The answer depends on information the model cannot see
A wrong answer would be costly and nothing checks it

/ai/foundations/tokens-and-context-windo.def: A token is the small piece of text a model reads and writes, roughly four characters of English. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can handle in one call, counting your input and its answer together.
/ai/foundations/tokens-and-context-windo.why: Models cannot work on raw letters or unlimited text. Splitting text into tokens gives a fixed vocabulary to work with, and the window limits how much one call can hold. Tokens are also what providers charge for.
use: You check whether a prompt fits before you send it
You estimate cost, speed or rate limits
You decide how much history and how many documents to include
avoid: You count characters or words and assume that is the limit
You fill the whole window because it is allowed
You reuse token counts from one model for another

/ai/foundations/credits-pricing-cost.def: LLM providers charge per token, with separate prices for input and output tokens. Credits are a prepaid balance that is spent as you use the service.
/ai/foundations/credits-pricing-cost.why: Running large models costs real compute for every token. Per-token pricing makes the bill follow usage, and prepaid credits let you cap what you can spend. Without tracking, one long prompt or one looping agent can use up the balance.
use: You plan the monthly cost of an AI feature before building it
You choose between a small and a large model
You set budgets and alerts per user or feature
avoid: You judge cost by the price per token alone, without counting tokens per call
You send the full history on every call without trimming
You hard-code prices that providers change often

/ai/prompting/prompt-engineering.def: Prompt engineering is writing the input to a model so that it gives useful, reliable output. A good prompt states the task, gives the needed context and examples, and says what format to answer in.
/ai/prompting/prompt-engineering.why: A model does exactly what the text tells it, so unclear instructions give unclear answers. Better prompts improve results without retraining the model, which makes them the cheapest first thing to try.
use: The model gives the right kind of answer but not reliably
You need a fixed output format that your code can read
You want to improve quality without changing the model
avoid: The model lacks the information, since wording cannot add facts (use retrieval)
You judge a prompt from one or two answers
The prompt keeps growing with patches after every bug

/ai/prompting/context-engineering.def: Context engineering is choosing what information the model sees on each call: instructions, tools, documents, history and memory. The aim is the smallest set of information that lets the model do the task well.
/ai/prompting/context-engineering.why: Prompts alone are not enough once an application runs many steps. The context fills with history and tool results, which costs money, slows calls and distracts the model. Managing it on purpose keeps answers accurate.
use: The application runs many steps or long conversations (agents, chat)
You add documents or tool results to the model input
Answers get worse or costs grow as sessions get longer
avoid: The task is a single short call, where plain prompt wording is enough
You add everything just in case
You keep every old tool result in the history

/ai/retrieval/embeddings-vector-database.def: An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a text, so texts with similar meaning have similar numbers. A vector database stores embeddings and quickly finds the ones closest to a query.
/ai/retrieval/embeddings-vector-database.why: Keyword search misses answers that use different words, such as "money back" versus "refund". Embeddings let you search by meaning, and a vector database makes that fast on large collections.
use: You search by meaning rather than exact words
You build retrieval for RAG
You find similar items (documents, products, questions)
avoid: You need exact matches for ids, codes or names (use keyword search or both)
You have only a few documents that fit in the prompt
You would add a separate vector engine before checking whether pgvector is enough

/ai/retrieval/rag.def: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means finding the most relevant pieces of your own data and putting them in the prompt, so the model answers from them. The model uses your documents instead of relying only on what it learned in training.
/ai/retrieval/rag.why: A model does not know your private documents or recent events, and it may invent answers when it lacks facts. RAG supplies the facts at question time without retraining, and lets you show sources.
use: Answers must come from private or frequently changing documents
Users need sources they can check
The knowledge base is too large to put in every prompt
avoid: You want to change the model's style or behaviour (use prompting or fine-tuning)
Only a few short documents are needed (put them straight into the prompt)
You have no way to test whether retrieval finds the right text

/ai/agents/ai-agents.def: An AI agent is a program where an LLM decides the next step in a loop, using tools. The model asks for an action, your code runs it, the result goes back to the model, and this repeats until the task is done or a limit is reached.
/ai/agents/ai-agents.why: Some tasks cannot be written as fixed steps, because what to do next depends on what was just found. An agent lets the model choose the steps, so one system can handle open-ended work. That freedom needs limits to stay safe and affordable.
use: The steps depend on what is found along the way (research, debugging, multi-step lookups)
The task needs several tools combined
A person can review risky actions
avoid: The steps are known in advance (use a fixed workflow: cheaper and more predictable)
A mistake is costly and cannot be approved or undone
You cannot set step, budget and permission limits

/ai/foundations/fine-tuning-and-model-ch.def: Fine-tuning means training an existing model further on your own examples, so its behaviour, style or format changes. Choosing a model means testing candidates on your task and picking the cheapest one that is good enough.
/ai/foundations/fine-tuning-and-model-ch.why: A general model is not always right for your task, and the largest model is slow and costly. Fine-tuning adapts behaviour, and careful model choice and routing keep quality up and cost down.
use: A prompt cannot give you a consistent style, format or narrow skill
A small model must match a large one on one task (distillation)
You choose or switch models and want evidence from your own tests
avoid: You want to teach facts that change (use RAG)
You have not tried a better prompt first
You pick a model from a leaderboard without testing your own cases

/ai/prompting/structured-output-and-tool.def: Structured output makes a model reply in a fixed shape, usually JSON that your code can read. Tool calling lets the model ask your code to run a function, and then continue with the result.
/ai/prompting/structured-output-and-tool.why: A program cannot do much with a paragraph of prose, and a model alone cannot look things up or change anything. These two features let a model fit into normal software: it returns data you can parse and asks for actions you can control.
use: Your code needs a label, number or record from the model
The model needs live data or must trigger an action
You want to validate and limit what the model can do
avoid: A plain text answer is enough
You would pass model-made arguments straight to a database, shell or URL
You give the model many overlapping tools

/ai/agents/model-context-protocol.def: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. A server exposes tools, resources and prompts, and any MCP-capable application can use them.
/ai/agents/model-context-protocol.why: Without a standard, every AI application needs a custom connector for every tool, so the work multiplies. With MCP you write a connector once as a server and many applications can use it.
use: You want one tool or data source available to several AI applications
You use ready-made servers for common systems
You want a standard way to describe tools to agents
avoid: One application needs one simple function (a normal tool is enough)
You would install a server you cannot trust or review
You connect many servers and flood the context with tool descriptions

/ai/agents/multi-agent-patterns.def: A multi-agent system uses several model-driven agents that work together, each with its own instructions, tools and context. Common patterns are orchestrator and workers, pipelines, parallel work, routers and evaluator loops.
/ai/agents/multi-agent-patterns.why: One agent can run out of context, cannot do independent work in parallel, and holds all permissions at once. Splitting the work solves those problems, at the price of more tokens and more to manage.
use: One context cannot hold the work
Sub-tasks are independent and can run in parallel
Different parts need different tools or permissions
avoid: A single agent or a fixed workflow would work
You cannot cap steps and budget for each agent
The hand-offs would be long free text

/ai/safety/guardrails-and-safety.def: Guardrails are checks and limits in your code around a model: on inputs, outputs, actions and resource use. The model suggests, and your code decides what is allowed.
/ai/safety/guardrails-and-safety.why: A model can be wrong, can be tricked and can ignore instructions in a prompt. Code checks are the only reliable way to stop a bad output or action from causing harm.
use: The model can trigger actions or show text to users
Mistakes would be costly or hard to undo
You need an audit trail of what was allowed or blocked
avoid: You rely on the prompt alone to enforce rules
Filters block so much that users work around them
Everything is allowed except a short banned list

/ai/safety/prompt-injection-and-security.def: Prompt injection is when text from an untrusted source contains instructions and the model follows them. It can come from the user (direct) or hide in content the model reads, such as a web page or email (indirect).
/ai/safety/prompt-injection-and-security.why: A model treats instructions and data as the same thing, text, and cannot reliably tell them apart. So untrusted content can steer it, and the system must be designed so that even a fooled model cannot do serious harm.
use: The model reads outside content (web, email, documents, tool results)
The model has tools that send data or change things
You review an AI feature for security
avoid: You trust a firm sentence in the system prompt as protection
One session has private data, untrusted content and outbound actions together
Tools run with system-wide rights instead of the user's

/ai/production/evals-and-testing.def: Evals are repeatable tests that run an LLM feature over many realistic cases and score the results. They show whether a change made things better or worse.
/ai/production/evals-and-testing.why: Model answers vary, and a small change to a prompt, model or document can shift results across many cases. A few manual tries cannot show that, so you measure on a fixed set.
use: Before changing a prompt, model, retrieval or tool
To gate releases in your build pipeline
To compare models and prompt versions on your own cases
avoid: You judge a change from two or three examples
The set has only easy cases
You trust a model judge without checking it against people

/ai/production/observability-latency-cac.def: Observability means recording enough about every model call (tokens, latency, cost, prompt version, tool calls) to explain what happened. Latency work and caching make the feature faster and cheaper.
/ai/production/observability-latency-cac.why: Model calls are slow, costly and variable. Without records you cannot explain a wrong or slow answer, or a surprising bill, and without caching and limits you pay for repeated work and fail under rate limits.
use: Any LLM feature in production
You need to find the cause of slow or wrong answers
You need to control cost and survive provider limits and outages
avoid: You log full prompts with personal data and keep them forever
You use semantic caching with a loose threshold
You cache private answers without the user in the key

/ai/production/spring-ai-and-langchain4j.def: Spring AI and LangChain4j are Java libraries for working with LLMs. They handle messages, structured output, tools, RAG, memory and many providers, so you do not write that plumbing yourself.
/ai/production/spring-ai-and-langchain4j.why: Calling a model API directly means repeating the same code for messages, parsing, the tool loop and vector stores. A library does that once and lets you switch providers more easily.
use: You build Java services that call LLMs (Spring AI for Spring Boot, LangChain4j for any Java)
You need tools, RAG or structured output quickly
You want one interface over several providers
avoid: You spread library types through all business code
You copy examples written for another version
You let the library run tool loops with no limits

/system-design/design-a-rag-chatbot.def: A RAG chatbot answers employee questions from company documents. An ingestion pipeline builds a searchable index, and for each question the system retrieves allowed chunks, builds a prompt and generates an answer with citations.
/system-design/design-a-rag-chatbot.why: Employees cannot find answers across thousands of documents, and a plain model does not know the company's private or changing information. RAG supplies the right text at question time, with sources and permission checks.
use: Answers must come from private or changing documents
Users need citations they can check
Different users may read different documents
avoid: A few short documents fit in the prompt
You cannot enforce permissions at retrieval
Nobody will measure answer quality

/system-design/design-an-ai-agent-platfo.def: An AI agent platform runs agents for many teams. It queues runs, executes the agent loop with saved state, routes model calls through a gateway, runs tools in sandboxes, asks humans for approval and tracks cost and traces.
/system-design/design-an-ai-agent-platfo.why: Every team building agents alone would repeat the same hard parts: crash recovery, safety, limits, credentials and cost control. A shared platform solves them once and keeps teams isolated.
use: Several teams run agents and need shared limits, safety and accounting
Runs are long, call many tools and sometimes wait for approval
You need audit, cost control and isolation
avoid: One team has one simple agent (a library is enough)
You would build a platform before you know what agents you need
You cannot staff it or buy it managed

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/encapsula.def: Encapsulation means keeping an object's data private and letting other code change it only through methods. The object can then protect its own rules, so it never ends up in an invalid state.

example.title: A bank account that protects its balance

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/abstracti.def: Abstraction means showing what something does and hiding how it does it. In Java you describe the "what" with an interface or an abstract class, and callers depend on that instead of on a concrete class.

example.title: Checkout does not care how the payment is made

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/inheritan.def: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another class with `extends`. The child class gets the parent's fields and methods and can add new ones or change existing ones. Use it for a true "is-a" relationship.

example.title: A manager is an employee with extras

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/polymorph.def: Polymorphism means one call can run different code depending on the real object. You call a method on a parent type, and Java picks the child's version while the program runs.

example.title: One loop, three different areas

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/compositi.def: Composition means building a class by holding other objects and using them, instead of extending a class. It keeps classes loosely coupled and easy to change, so it is usually preferred over inheritance when you only want to reuse behaviour.

example.title: A notifier that can swap how it sends messages

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/interface.def: An interface describes what a type can do and holds no state. An abstract class can also hold shared fields and partly finished code. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.

example.title: An abstract base class plus an interface

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/single-re.def: The single responsibility principle says a class should have one reason to change. Each class does one job, so a change to one concern does not break another.

example.title: Calculating an invoice and printing it are two jobs

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/open-clos.def: The open/closed principle says code should be open for extension but closed for modification. You add new behaviour by adding new classes, not by editing code that already works.

example.title: Adding a new discount without touching the checkout

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/liskov-su.def: The Liskov substitution principle says a child class must work anywhere its parent is expected, without surprising the caller. If code that works with the parent breaks when it gets the child, the hierarchy is wrong.

example.title: A Square that breaks code written for Rectangle, and a fix

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/interface.def: The interface segregation principle says no class should be forced to implement methods it does not use. Prefer several small interfaces over one big one.

example.title: A basic printer is not forced to scan

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/dependenc.def: The dependency inversion principle says high-level code should depend on an abstraction, not on a concrete class. The concrete class is passed in from outside, which makes it easy to swap and to test.

example.title: A service that gets its sender from outside

/java/core-java/generics/generic-classes.def: A generic class works with a type that you choose when you use it, written like `Box<String>`. The compiler checks the type for you, so you do not need casts.

example.title: A box that holds any one type, and a pair of two types

/java/core-java/generics/generic-methods.def: A generic method has its own type parameter, written before the return type. Java works out the type from the arguments, so one method can serve many types safely.

example.title: One method that works for any list or array

/java/core-java/generics/bounded-types.def: A bounded type parameter limits which types are allowed, using `extends`. Inside the method you can then call the methods of the bound, such as `compareTo`.

example.title: A max method that only accepts things that can be compared

/java/core-java/generics/wildcards.def: A wildcard `?` stands for "some unknown type". `? extends Number` means "Number or any subtype", which is good for reading. `?` alone means any type at all.

example.title: Summing a list of any number type

/java/core-java/generics/pecs.def: PECS means: if a collection only gives you values, use `? extends T` (producer extends). If it only receives values, use `? super T` (consumer super). It makes a method accept more types while staying type-safe.

example.title: Copy from a producer into a consumer

/java/core-java/generics/type-erasure.def: Type erasure means generic type arguments exist only at compile time. At run time `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both just `List`, so you cannot ask a list what type it holds.

example.title: Two different lists, the same class at run time

/java/core-java/exceptions/checked-vs-un.def: A checked exception must be caught or declared with `throws`, so the compiler makes you deal with it. An unchecked exception (a `RuntimeException`) needs no declaration and usually means a bug in the code.

example.title: Reading a missing file (checked) and bad input (unchecked)

/java/core-java/exceptions/try-catch-fin.def: Code that might fail goes in `try`. `catch` handles a specific problem, and `finally` always runs afterwards, whether or not an exception happened. Catch the most specific exception first.

example.title: Parsing a number, with cleanup that always runs

/java/core-java/exceptions/try-with-reso.def: try-with-resources closes things like files and connections for you, even when an exception happens. The resource must implement `AutoCloseable`. If both the body and `close` fail, the close error is attached to the first one as a suppressed exception.

example.title: A resource that is closed automatically, in reverse order

/java/core-java/exceptions/custom-except.def: A custom exception is your own exception class, named after the problem, such as `InsufficientFundsException`. It can carry extra data so the caller knows exactly what went wrong.

example.title: An exception that carries the missing amount

/java/core-java/exceptions/exception-cha.def: Exception chaining means wrapping a low-level exception inside a higher-level one and keeping the original as its cause. The caller gets a meaningful message, and the full story is still available through `getCause()`.

example.title: Wrapping a parse error in a service error

/java/core-java/exceptions/multi-catch.def: A multi-catch handles several exception types in one block, written `catch (A | B e)`. Use it when the handling is the same. You can also rethrow an exception after logging it, so callers still see the failure.

example.title: One handler for two kinds of failure

/java/core-java/immutability/immutable-c.def: An immutable class creates objects that never change. Make the class `final`, make all fields `private final`, set them in the constructor, and give no setters. Methods that "change" the object return a new one.

example.title: A Money class where plus() returns a new object

/java/core-java/immutability/defensive-c.def: A defensive copy means copying a mutable object when it goes into or comes out of your class. Without it, the caller keeps a reference to your internal data and can change it behind your back, even if the field is `final`.

example.title: Copying a list on the way in, and exposing a read-only view

/java/core-java/immutability/immutable-c.def: `List.of`, `Set.of` and `Map.of` create collections that cannot be changed. `List.copyOf` makes an independent immutable snapshot, while `Collections.unmodifiableList` is only a read-only window onto a list that can still change.

example.title: List.copyOf is a snapshot, unmodifiableList is a live view

/java/core-java/immutability/withers.def: A "wither" is a method that returns a copy of an immutable object with one value changed, for example `withEmail(...)`. It gives you the convenience of updating without making the object mutable.

example.title: Changing one field by creating a modified copy

/java/core-java/immutability/string-immu.def: A Java `String` can never be changed after it is created. Methods like `toUpperCase()` or `replace()` return a new String and leave the original alone. Use `StringBuilder` when you build text in a loop.

example.title: String methods return new strings; StringBuilder changes in place

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/lamb.def: A lambda is a short piece of code you can pass around, written `(input) -> result`. It replaces a bulky anonymous class when an interface has just one method.

example.title: Sorting with a lambda instead of an anonymous class

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/func.def: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, so a lambda can stand in for it. Java provides common ones: `Function` (input to output), `Predicate` (yes or no), `Supplier` (gives a value) and `Consumer` (uses a value).

example.title: The four built-in shapes, and your own

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/meth.def: A method reference is a shorter lambda that just calls an existing method, written `Class::method`. Use it when the lambda would only pass its argument straight to that method.

example.title: Replacing small lambdas with method references

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/map-.def: A stream is a pipeline for data. `filter` keeps items that match, `map` changes each item, and `collect` or `toList` gathers the result. Nothing runs until that final step.

example.title: Names of adults, in capitals

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/grou.def: Collectors turn a stream into a result. `groupingBy` splits items into groups, `counting` counts them, `joining` builds one string, and `toMap` builds a map.

example.title: Group words by length, count them, and join them

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/flat.def: `flatMap` turns each item into a stream and joins all of those streams into one. Use it when each item holds a list and you want one flat list of everything.

example.title: From a list of orders to one list of items

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/redu.def: `reduce` combines all items of a stream into a single value by applying an operation again and again, such as adding numbers. It needs a starting value and a rule for combining two values.

example.title: Adding numbers, and finding the longest word

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/opti.def: `Optional` is a box that holds a value or is empty. It makes "there may be no result" visible in the method signature, so callers must decide what to do instead of hitting a `NullPointerException`.

example.title: Finding a user that may not exist

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/para.def: A parallel stream splits the work across several CPU cores. It can speed up heavy calculations on large data, but it adds overhead, so it is slower for small lists. Never use it for blocking calls or with shared mutable state.

example.title: Same result, computed on several cores

/java/core-java/modern-java/var.def: `var` lets the compiler work out the type of a local variable from the value on the right, so you do not repeat a long type name. The variable is still strongly typed; it is just not written out.

example.title: Less typing, same safety

/java/core-java/modern-java/records.def: A record is a short way to declare a class that only carries data. You list the fields once, and Java creates the constructor, getters, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. The fields are final.

example.title: A data class in one line

/java/core-java/modern-java/text-blocks.def: A text block is a multi-line string written between triple quotes. It keeps line breaks and removes the common indentation, so JSON, SQL and HTML are easy to read in code without `\n` and escaped quotes.

example.title: A JSON string without escaping

/java/core-java/modern-java/switch-expre.def: A switch expression returns a value and uses `->`, so there is no fall-through and no `break`. The compiler checks that every case is covered, which makes it safer than the old switch statement.

example.title: Turning a day into a number of hours

/java/core-java/modern-java/sealed-class.def: A sealed class or interface lists exactly which classes may extend it, using `permits`. The compiler then knows every possible subtype, so a `switch` over it is checked for completeness without a `default`.

example.title: A closed set of payment types

/java/core-java/modern-java/default-and-.def: Since Java 8 an interface can contain methods with a body. A `default` method gives implementing classes a ready-made behaviour they may override, and a `static` method belongs to the interface itself. This let Java add new methods to old interfaces without breaking existing classes.

example.title: An interface with a default method and a static helper

/java/core-java/modern-java/date-and-tim.def: The `java.time` package (Java 8) replaced the old `Date` and `Calendar`. Its classes, such as `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime`, `Duration` and `Period`, are immutable and clear, and they handle months, days and formatting correctly.

example.title: Adding months, measuring days and formatting a date

/java/core-java/modern-java/collection-f.def: `List.of`, `Set.of` and `Map.of` (Java 9) create small immutable collections in one line. They do not allow `null`, and `Set.of` and `Map.of` reject duplicates.

example.title: Immutable collections in one line

/java/core-java/modern-java/private-inte.def: Since Java 9 an interface can have `private` methods. They let several default methods share code inside the interface without exposing that code to anyone else.

example.title: Two default methods sharing one private helper

/java/core-java/modern-java/stream-takew.def: `takeWhile` keeps items from the start of a stream until a condition first fails. `dropWhile` skips items from the start until the condition first fails and keeps the rest. Java 9 also added `Stream.iterate` with a stop condition.

example.title: Cutting a stream at the first item that fails a test

/java/core-java/modern-java/optional-add.def: Java 9 added `ifPresentOrElse` (do one thing if there is a value, another if not), `or` (try another Optional) and `stream` (turn an Optional into a stream of zero or one items).

example.title: Handling both cases without an if statement

/java/core-java/modern-java/try-with-res.def: Before Java 9 a resource had to be declared inside the `try (...)` parentheses. Now you can pass a variable that already exists, as long as it is final or effectively final, and Java still closes it for you.

example.title: Using an existing variable as the resource

/java/core-java/modern-java/modules.def: The Java Platform Module System (Java 9) groups packages into named modules. A `module-info.java` file says what the module needs (`requires`) and which packages other modules may use (`exports`), so internal packages stay hidden.

example.title: A module that exports one package and keeps another internal

/java/core-java/modern-java/copyof-and-u.def: Java 10 added `List.copyOf`, `Set.copyOf` and `Map.copyOf` to make an immutable copy of an existing collection. It also added `Collectors.toUnmodifiableList`, `toUnmodifiableSet` and `toUnmodifiableMap` for streams.

example.title: Copying a list and collecting a stream into an immutable list

/java/core-java/modern-java/string-metho.def: Java 11 added useful `String` methods: `isBlank` (empty or only spaces), `strip` (trim that understands Unicode), `lines` (split into lines as a stream) and `repeat`.

example.title: The four new String helpers

/java/core-java/modern-java/http-client.def: Java 11 made `java.net.http.HttpClient` a standard part of Java. It sends HTTP requests, supports HTTP/2, and can work synchronously or asynchronously, so you no longer need an extra library for simple calls.

example.title: Calling a small local server (so it runs without internet)

/java/core-java/modern-java/files-readst.def: Java 11 added `Files.readString` and `Files.writeString` to read or write a whole text file in one line, with UTF-8 by default.

example.title: Write a file and read it back

/java/core-java/modern-java/predicate-no.def: `Predicate.not` (Java 11) reverses a condition so you can use it with a method reference, for example `filter(Predicate.not(String::isBlank))` instead of writing a lambda with `!`.

example.title: Keeping only the non-blank lines

/java/core-java/modern-java/var-in-lambd.def: Java 11 lets you write `var` for lambda parameters. It does not change behaviour, but it lets you add annotations such as `@NonNull` to a parameter without writing out its type.

example.title: Using var for lambda parameters

/java/core-java/modern-java/single-file-.def: Java 11 can run a `.java` file directly with `java Hello.java`. It compiles the file in memory and runs it, which is handy for small scripts and for learning.

example.title: One file, one command

/java/core-java/modern-java/collectors-t.def: `Collectors.teeing` (Java 12) runs two collectors over the same stream at once and combines their two results. It saves you from going through the data twice.

example.title: Count and total in one pass, then compute the average

/java/core-java/modern-java/string-inden.def: Java 12 added `String.indent` (add or remove leading spaces on every line) and `String.transform` (pass a string through a function so you can chain steps).

example.title: Indenting text and chaining a transformation

/java/core-java/modern-java/helpful-npe-.def: Since Java 14 (on by default from Java 15) a `NullPointerException` tells you exactly which part was null, for example "because the return value of Demo.findCity() is null". You no longer have to guess in a long chain of calls.

example.title: The exception now names the null part

/java/core-java/modern-java/pattern-matc.def: Pattern matching for `instanceof` (Java 16) checks a type and gives you a typed variable in one step. You no longer need a separate cast after the check.

example.title: No cast after instanceof

/java/core-java/modern-java/stream-tolis.def: `Stream.toList()` (Java 16) ends a stream with an unmodifiable list, so you no longer write `collect(Collectors.toList())` for the common case.

example.title: A shorter way to finish a stream

/java/core-java/modern-java/random-gener.def: Java 17 added the `RandomGenerator` interface and a factory with many modern algorithms. You pick an algorithm by name and can seed it, so the same seed always gives the same numbers.

example.title: A seeded generator gives repeatable numbers

/java/core-java/modern-java/utf8-by-defa.def: Since Java 18 the default character set of the JVM is UTF-8 on every operating system. Before, it depended on the machine (for example Windows-1252), so the same code could read text differently on different computers.

example.title: The default charset is now always UTF-8

/java/core-java/modern-java/virtual-thre.def: Virtual threads (Java 21) are very cheap threads managed by the JVM. When one waits, for example on a network call, it steps aside so another can run. You can run tens of thousands at once with simple blocking code.

example.title: 10,000 tasks that each wait, run at the same time

/java/core-java/modern-java/pattern-matc.def: Pattern matching for `switch` (Java 21) lets a `switch` choose code by the type of a value, and even add a condition with `when`. It also handles `null` as a case.

example.title: A switch that picks code by type and condition

/java/core-java/modern-java/record-patte.def: A record pattern (Java 21) takes a record apart inside `instanceof` or `switch`, giving you its fields as variables. Patterns can be nested, so you can unpack a record that holds other records in one step.

example.title: Unpacking a Line made of two Points

/java/core-java/modern-java/sequenced-co.def: Sequenced collections (Java 21) add a common way to work with the first and last element and to reverse any collection that has a defined order. New methods include `getFirst`, `getLast`, `addFirst`, `addLast` and `reversed`.

example.title: First, last and reversed on a list and a LinkedHashMap

/java/core-java/modern-java/unnamed-vari.def: An underscore `_` (Java 22) marks a variable you must declare but will never use, such as a loop variable, a caught exception or a part of a pattern. It tells the reader, and the compiler, that the value is ignored on purpose.

example.title: Underscore for values you do not need

/java/core-java/modern-java/markdown-doc.def: Since Java 23 you can write documentation comments in Markdown by starting each line with `///` instead of the old `/** ... */` with HTML. Lists, bold, links and code blocks use normal Markdown.

example.title: A documentation comment written in Markdown

/java/core-java/modern-java/stream-gathe.def: A gatherer (Java 24) is a custom step in a stream pipeline that can group, window or carry state between items, which the old `map` and `filter` could not do. `Gatherers` ships ready-made ones such as `windowFixed` and `windowSliding`.

example.title: Grouping items into windows

/java/core-java/modern-java/scoped-value.def: A scoped value (Java 25) shares data with the code you call, for example the current user, without passing it as a parameter. The value is fixed for the duration of one `run` and is safe to share with virtual threads, which makes it a cleaner replacement for `ThreadLocal`.

example.title: The current user, available to every method inside run()

/java/core-java/modern-java/flexible-con.def: Flexible constructor bodies (Java 25) let you run statements before calling `super(...)` or `this(...)`, as long as they do not use the object being built. You can validate or compute arguments first instead of using awkward static helper methods.

example.title: Validating an argument before calling super

/java/core-java/modern-java/module-impor.def: A module import (Java 25) imports every public class that a module exports with one line, `import module java.base;`. It saves long lists of imports in small programs and scripts.

example.title: One import line instead of five

/java/core-java/modern-java/compact-sour.def: Compact source files (Java 25) let a small program be just a `void main()` method, with no class declaration and no `public static`. It removes the ceremony from a first program or a script.

example.title: A whole program with no class around it

/java/core-java/collections-framework/ar.def: A `List` keeps items in order and allows duplicates. `ArrayList` stores items in an array, so reading by position is fast. `LinkedList` chains nodes together, so adding at the ends is fast but reading by position is slow. Choose `ArrayList` almost every time.

example.title: The same list operations on both

/java/core-java/collections-framework/se.def: A `Set` holds no duplicates. `HashSet` has no defined order and is the fastest. `LinkedHashSet` keeps insertion order. `TreeSet` keeps items sorted. Pick by the order you need.

example.title: Three sets, three orders

/java/core-java/collections-framework/ma.def: A `Map` stores key-value pairs with unique keys. `HashMap` is fast with no order, `LinkedHashMap` remembers insertion order, and `TreeMap` keeps keys sorted. The choice is again about the order you need.

example.title: Iterating the same data in three orders

/java/core-java/collections-framework/qu.def: A `Queue` hands items out in the order they arrive (first in, first out). A `PriorityQueue` hands out the smallest item first. A `Deque` works at both ends, so `ArrayDeque` can act as a queue or as a stack.

example.title: FIFO queue, priority queue and stack

/java/core-java/collections-framework/co.def: `Comparable` gives a class its natural order through `compareTo`. A `Comparator` defines a different order from the outside, so you can sort the same objects in several ways. `Comparator.comparing` builds one from a field.

example.title: Natural order, then custom orders

/java/core-java/collections-framework/it.def: An `Iterator` walks a collection one item at a time and is the safe way to remove items while looping. Most collections are fail-fast: if you change them during a `for-each` loop, they throw `ConcurrentModificationException`.

example.title: The wrong way to remove while looping, and two right ways

/java/core-java/collections-framework/co.def: The `Collections` class has ready-made helpers for lists and other collections: sorting, shuffling with a seed, counting, finding the largest, reversing, and creating read-only views.

example.title: Handy one-liners

/java/core-java/equals-hashcode/equals-c.def: `equals` says when two objects count as the same value. A correct `equals` is reflexive (x equals x), symmetric (if x equals y then y equals x), transitive, consistent and never true for `null`. Always take an `Object` parameter so you really override it.

example.title: A correct equals method

/java/core-java/equals-hashcode/hashcode.def: `hashCode` turns an object into a number that hash collections use to find it quickly. The rule: if two objects are equal, they must return the same hash code. Different objects may share a hash code, but a good spread keeps collections fast.

example.title: Equal objects, same hash code

/java/core-java/equals-hashcode/missing-.def: If you override `equals` but not `hashCode`, two equal objects usually get different hash codes. A `HashSet` or `HashMap` then looks in the wrong bucket, so it usually cannot find an object that is equal to one it already holds, and duplicates can appear.

example.title: Equal objects with different hash codes, and the fix

/java/core-java/equals-hashcode/mutable-.def: If a field used by `hashCode` changes after the object is stored in a `HashMap` or `HashSet`, the object sits in the wrong bucket and can no longer be found. Use immutable objects (or records) as keys.

example.title: A key that changes after it was stored

/java/core-java/equals-hashcode/objects-.def: `Objects.equals` and `Objects.hash` make `equals` and `hashCode` short and null-safe. A `record` goes further: Java writes correct `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` for you from the fields.

example.title: Hand-written, with Objects helpers, and with a record

/java/core-java/hashmap-internals/bucket.def: A `HashMap` keeps its entries in an array of buckets. To pick a bucket it takes the key's `hashCode`, mixes the high bits into the low bits, and keeps only the low bits with a bit mask. That is how it jumps straight to the right place without searching.

example.title: How a key becomes a bucket number (simplified from the JDK source)

/java/core-java/hashmap-internals/collis.def: A collision happens when two different keys land in the same bucket. The `HashMap` keeps them together in a chain and uses `equals` to tell them apart, so the map still works, but a lookup has to compare against more entries.

example.title: Keys with the same hash share one bucket and cost extra equals calls

/java/core-java/hashmap-internals/presiz.def: A `HashMap` starts with 16 buckets and grows (doubles) when it is more than 75% full, which is its load factor. Growing means rebuilding the table, so if you know how many entries are coming, create the map with the right size from the start.

example.title: Sizing a map for 1,000 entries without resizing

/java/core-java/hashmap-internals/null-k.def: `HashMap` allows one `null` key and any number of `null` values. `TreeMap` and `ConcurrentHashMap` do not allow a `null` key, and `ConcurrentHashMap` does not allow `null` values either, because a `null` result from `get` would then be ambiguous.

example.title: Which maps accept null

/java/core-java/hashmap-internals/iterat.def: A `HashMap` does not promise any iteration order, so never depend on it. It is also fail-fast: changing the map while looping over it throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. Remove entries with an iterator or `removeIf`.

example.title: Removing entries safely while iterating

/java/core-java/concurrenthashmap/merge-.def: `merge` and `compute` update the value for one key as a single atomic step, so several threads can safely count or update without losing changes. A separate `get` followed by `put` is two steps and can lose updates.

example.title: Four threads counting into one map

/java/core-java/concurrenthashmap/comput.def: `putIfAbsent` stores a value only if the key is missing. `computeIfAbsent` also builds the value only when it is missing, and does it once even if many threads ask at the same time. That makes it a simple, safe cache.

example.title: A cache that loads each key only once

/java/core-java/concurrenthashmap/bulk-o.def: `ConcurrentHashMap` has bulk methods that can run in parallel: `forEach`, `search` and `reduce`. You give a parallelism threshold: the map only splits the work across threads when it is bigger than that number.

example.title: Totalling and searching a map in parallel

/java/core-java/concurrenthashmap/no-nul.def: `ConcurrentHashMap` rejects `null` keys and `null` values. In a concurrent map, a `null` returned from `get` must mean "no such key". If `null` values were allowed you could not tell the two cases apart without another call that another thread may change.

example.title: null is rejected on purpose

/java/core-java/concurrenthashmap/synchr.def: `Collections.synchronizedMap` wraps any map with one lock, so only one thread works at a time and you must still lock by hand when you loop or combine steps. `ConcurrentHashMap` locks only a small part and has atomic methods, so it scales much better.

example.title: The extra locking a synchronized map needs

/java/concurrency-jvm/threads-basics/cre.def: A thread is one path of execution. You create one by giving a `Thread` some code to run (a `Runnable`, usually a lambda) and calling `start()`. Call `join()` to wait until it has finished.

example.title: Three threads each compute a result, and main waits for them

/java/concurrency-jvm/threads-basics/thr.def: A thread is in one of a few states: `NEW` (created, not started), `RUNNABLE` (running or ready), `BLOCKED` (waiting for a lock), `WAITING` or `TIMED_WAITING` (waiting for another thread or a timer), and `TERMINATED` (finished).

example.title: Watching one thread move through its states

/java/concurrency-jvm/threads-basics/int.def: You cannot safely force a thread to stop. Instead you ask it to stop by calling `interrupt()`. The thread checks `isInterrupted()` (or catches `InterruptedException` from `sleep` or `wait`) and ends itself cleanly.

example.title: Asking a worker to stop

/java/concurrency-jvm/threads-basics/dae.def: A daemon thread is a background helper. The JVM does not wait for daemon threads: when only daemon threads are left, the program ends. Normal (non-daemon) threads keep the program alive until they finish.

example.title: A daemon thread does not keep the program alive

/java/concurrency-jvm/threads-basics/thr.def: A `ThreadLocal` gives every thread its own copy of a value. It is handy for per-thread context such as the current user or a non-thread-safe helper, but values must be removed when you are done, especially in thread pools.

example.title: Each thread sees only its own value

/java/concurrency-jvm/threads-basics/dea.def: A deadlock happens when two threads each hold a lock the other one needs, so both wait forever. You avoid it by always taking locks in the same order, or by using `tryLock` with a timeout so a thread can give up.

example.title: Two threads that would deadlock, saved by a timeout

/java/concurrency-jvm/synchronization-an.def: `synchronized` lets only one thread at a time run a block of code, using the lock of an object. It protects shared data that several threads change, so updates are not lost.

example.title: A counter that stays correct with two threads

/java/concurrency-jvm/synchronization-an.def: A `volatile` field is always read from and written to main memory, so a change made by one thread becomes visible to the others straight away. It guarantees visibility, but not that compound steps such as `count++` are atomic.

example.title: A stop flag that another thread is guaranteed to see

/java/concurrency-jvm/synchronization-an.def: Atomic classes such as `AtomicInteger` update one value safely without a lock, using a hardware instruction called compare-and-swap. `LongAdder` is even faster when many threads only add to a counter.

example.title: Counting from many threads without locks

/java/concurrency-jvm/synchronization-an.def: `ReentrantLock` is an explicit lock you take with `lock()` and release in a `finally` block. Compared with `synchronized` it can also try for a lock without waiting (`tryLock`), give up after a timeout, and be interrupted while waiting.

example.title: lock in try/finally, and tryLock

/java/concurrency-jvm/synchronization-an.def: A `ReadWriteLock` allows many threads to read at the same time, but only one thread to write, and no readers while it writes. It speeds up data that is read often and changed rarely.

example.title: A small cache with shared reads and exclusive writes

/java/concurrency-jvm/synchronization-an.def: A `CountDownLatch` makes a thread wait until other threads have finished a set number of steps. A `Semaphore` limits how many threads may use something at the same time, such as 3 database connections.

example.title: Wait for three workers, and allow only two at a time

/java/concurrency-jvm/synchronization-an.def: A `BlockingQueue` passes work between threads safely. `put` waits when the queue is full and `take` waits when it is empty, so a producer and a consumer can run at their own speed without any manual locking.

example.title: One producer, one consumer

/java/concurrency-jvm/memory-model/happe.def: "Happens-before" is the rule that says when one thread is guaranteed to see what another thread wrote. Starting a thread, joining it, releasing a lock and writing a `volatile` field all create such a guarantee. Without one, a thread may see old values.

example.title: start() and join() make writes visible

/java/concurrency-jvm/memory-model/volat.def: Without `volatile`, a thread may keep a stale copy of a field in a CPU cache or a register and never notice that another thread changed it. A write to a `volatile` field happens-before every later read of it, so the reader sees the update and everything written before it.

example.title: A flag publishes the data written before it

/java/concurrency-jvm/memory-model/safe-.def: Safe publication means handing an object to other threads so they see it fully built. Objects whose fields are `final` are safe to share even through a plain field, because Java guarantees other threads see the final fields set by the constructor.

example.title: An immutable object shared between threads

/java/concurrency-jvm/memory-model/doubl.def: Double-checked locking creates a shared object lazily and checks twice, once without a lock for speed and once with it for safety. It only works if the field is `volatile`; otherwise another thread can see a half-built object.

example.title: A lazy singleton that is correct

/java/concurrency-jvm/executors/fixed-th.def: An executor runs tasks for you on a pool of reusable threads. A fixed thread pool has a set number of threads: extra tasks wait in a queue until a thread is free. You submit work and the pool handles the threads.

example.title: Ten tasks on three threads

/java/concurrency-jvm/executors/threadpo.def: `ThreadPoolExecutor` lets you set the core size, the maximum size, the queue and what to do when it is full. Tasks first fill the core threads, then wait in the queue, and only when the queue is full are extra threads started. If everything is full, the rejection policy decides.

example.title: A small pool that rejects work when it is full

/java/concurrency-jvm/executors/schedule.def: A `ScheduledExecutorService` runs a task after a delay or repeatedly at a fixed rate. It replaces older `Timer` code and keeps running other tasks even if one of them fails.

example.title: A task that runs three times, once a moment

/java/concurrency-jvm/executors/future-a.def: A `Callable` is a task that returns a value (a `Runnable` does not). When you submit it to an executor you get a `Future`: a receipt you can use later to get the result with `get()`, which waits if it is not ready, or to see that the task failed.

example.title: Submit tasks, then collect their results

/java/concurrency-jvm/executors/graceful.def: Always shut an executor down, or its threads keep the program alive. `shutdown()` stops accepting new tasks and lets queued ones finish. `awaitTermination` waits. If tasks take too long, `shutdownNow()` interrupts them.

example.title: The standard shutdown sequence

/java/concurrency-jvm/executors/forkjoin.def: The Fork/Join pool splits a big task into smaller ones (fork), runs them in parallel, and combines the results (join). Idle threads steal work from busy ones. Parallel streams use it behind the scenes.

example.title: Summing a large array by splitting it

/java/concurrency-jvm/completablefuture/.def: A `CompletableFuture` is a result that will be ready later. `supplyAsync` starts a task in the background. `thenApply` says what to do with the result when it arrives, so you build a chain of steps without blocking a thread to wait.

example.title: Start a task, then transform its result

/java/concurrency-jvm/completablefuture/.def: `thenCompose` chains a step that itself returns a `CompletableFuture`, so the second call depends on the first result. `thenCombine` joins two independent futures that run at the same time, once both are done.

example.title: A dependent call, and two independent calls combined

/java/concurrency-jvm/completablefuture/.def: `allOf` waits until every future in a group is done, which is how you run many calls in parallel and then collect them. `anyOf` finishes as soon as the first one finishes.

example.title: Run several calls in parallel and gather the results

/java/concurrency-jvm/completablefuture/.def: If a step in a chain fails, the exception travels down the chain and later steps are skipped. `exceptionally` supplies a fallback value. `handle` runs whether the step succeeded or failed. `join` throws the failure wrapped in a `CompletionException`.

example.title: A fallback value and a handle step

/java/concurrency-jvm/completablefuture/.def: Always limit how long you wait: `orTimeout` fails the future after a time, and `completeOnTimeout` gives a default value instead. For blocking work, pass your own executor to the `Async` methods instead of using the shared common pool.

example.title: A slow call that is cut off, running on a dedicated pool

/java/concurrency-jvm/virtual-threads/cr.def: Since Java 21 you can start a virtual thread with `Thread.startVirtualThread` or `Thread.ofVirtual()`. It is used like a normal thread, but it is very cheap, so you create one per task instead of sharing a small pool.

example.title: Three ways to start a virtual thread

/java/concurrency-jvm/virtual-threads/ex.def: The usual way to use virtual threads is an executor that starts a new virtual thread for every task. Because they are cheap you do not pool them. Using the executor in try-with-resources waits for all tasks before continuing.

example.title: Fetching 5 values at the same time with plain blocking code

/java/concurrency-jvm/virtual-threads/li.def: Virtual threads are cheap, but the things they call (a database, a payment API) are not. Instead of limiting the threads, limit the use of the scarce resource, for example with a `Semaphore`.

example.title: Many virtual threads, at most 3 using the database at once

/java/concurrency-jvm/garbage-collection.def: Objects live on the heap. Most objects die young, so the collector splits the heap into a young area, where new objects start and are cleaned often and cheaply, and an old area for objects that survive. Cleaning the young area is called a minor collection.

example.title: Creating garbage and watching the collector run

/java/concurrency-jvm/garbage-collection.def: The collector frees only objects that nothing can reach any more. A normal (strong) reference keeps an object alive. A `WeakReference` does not: once nothing else refers to the object, the collector may free it, which is useful for caches.

example.title: A weakly referenced object disappears after a collection

/java/concurrency-jvm/garbage-collection.def: Java frees unreachable objects, so a "leak" means objects you no longer need that are still reachable, for example items added to a static list that is never cleared. Keep caches bounded and remove listeners and entries when you are done.

example.title: An ever-growing static list, and a bounded cache instead

/java/concurrency-jvm/garbage-collection.def: Java has several garbage collectors. G1 is the default and balances speed and pauses. ZGC aims for very short pauses on large heaps. Parallel favours total throughput, and Serial is for tiny programs. You choose one with a single `-XX:+Use...GC` flag.

example.title: The flags for each collector
example.code:
# G1: the default on most machines. Balanced; tune with a pause goal
java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 -jar app.jar

# ZGC: very short pauses, even on very large heaps (generational by default in recent Java)
java -XX:+UseZGC -jar app.jar

# Parallel: highest total throughput, longer pauses (good for batch jobs)
java -XX:+UseParallelGC -jar app.jar

# Serial: one thread, for tiny containers and small tools
java -XX:+UseSerialGC -jar app.jar

/java/concurrency-jvm/garbage-collection.def: GC logging records every collection: when it happened, how long it paused and how much memory was freed. Turn it on in production so that you can answer "was it the garbage collector?" with evidence.

example.title: Writing a GC log and reading it
example.code:
# turn on GC logging, with time stamps, into a file
java -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar app.jar

# what to look at in gc.log:
#   - pause times (how long the application stopped)
#   - how often collections happen
#   - heap size after each collection: if it keeps growing, suspect a memory leak

/java/concurrency-jvm/jvm-tuning-diagnos.def: Every thread has its own stack that holds method calls and local variables. If calls nest too deeply, usually from a recursion that never stops, the stack runs out and Java throws `StackOverflowError`. The stack size is set with `-Xss`.

example.title: A runaway recursion is caught

/java/concurrency-jvm/jvm-tuning-diagnos.def: The heap is the memory for objects. `-Xms` sets its starting size and `-Xmx` its maximum. In containers, `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` sets the maximum as a share of the container memory. Leave room for memory outside the heap, such as thread stacks and metaspace.

example.title: Sizing the heap and getting a dump if it fills up
example.code:
# fixed numbers
java -Xms512m -Xmx2g -jar app.jar

# in a container: a share of the memory limit (leave the rest for stacks, metaspace and native memory)
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -jar app.jar

# on OutOfMemoryError: write a heap dump to analyse, then stop so the platform restarts the app
java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/heap.hprof -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError -jar app.jar

/java/concurrency-jvm/jvm-tuning-diagnos.def: `jcmd` talks to a running Java process by its process id. It can print thread stacks (to find deadlocks and stuck threads), show heap and class statistics, trigger a heap dump and start Flight Recorder, all without restarting the application.

example.title: Looking inside a running JVM
example.code:
jcmd                                   # list running Java processes and their ids

jcmd <pid> Thread.print                # all thread stacks; deadlocks are reported at the end
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info                # heap sizes and usage
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram          # which classes use the most memory
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof   # a heap dump to open in a tool such as Eclipse MAT
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/rec.jfr   # Flight Recorder: low-overhead profiling

/java/concurrency-jvm/jvm-tuning-diagnos.def: The JVM first runs your code by interpreting it, notices which methods are used a lot, and compiles those to fast machine code while the program runs. That is the JIT compiler. It is why Java programs start slower and then speed up (warm-up).

example.title: Seeing the JIT at work
example.code:
# print every method as the JIT compiles it
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -jar app.jar

# only the quick compiler (C1): faster start, lower peak speed. Useful for short-lived tools
java -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 -jar app.jar

# tip: benchmark after a warm-up period, or use a tool like JMH, or your numbers will be misleading

/spring/core/ioc-and-dependency-injectio.def: Inversion of control means the Spring container creates your objects (called beans), wires them together and manages them, instead of your code calling `new`. You describe the beans, and the `ApplicationContext` builds them and hands them to you.

example.title: Describe a bean, let the container build it

/spring/core/ioc-and-dependency-injectio.def: Constructor injection means a class lists what it needs as constructor parameters and Spring supplies them. It is the preferred style: the dependencies are visible, they can be `final`, and the class is easy to create in a plain unit test.

example.title: A service that receives its dependency through the constructor

/spring/core/ioc-and-dependency-injectio.def: When two beans implement the same interface, Spring does not know which to inject and fails. `@Primary` marks the default one. `@Qualifier("name")` picks a specific one at the injection point.

example.title: Two notifiers: one default, one chosen by name

/spring/core/ioc-and-dependency-injectio.def: Spring can inject every bean of a type at once, as a `List` or a `Map` keyed by bean name. That lets you add a new implementation without changing the code that uses them, for example a new payment method.

example.title: A list and a map of all discount rules

/spring/core/ioc-and-dependency-injectio.def: A circular dependency means A needs B and B needs A. With constructor injection Spring cannot build either one first, so it fails at startup. The real fix is to redesign (move the shared logic into a third class); `@Lazy` is a last resort.

example.title: The failure, and the redesign

/spring/core/ioc-and-dependency-injectio.def: Component scanning makes Spring search a package for classes marked `@Component` and register them as beans. `@Service`, `@Repository` and `@Controller` are the same thing with a clearer meaning, and `@Repository` also translates database exceptions.

example.title: Finding beans by scanning

/spring/core/bean-lifecycle-and-scopes/l.def: Spring creates a bean, injects its dependencies, then calls your `@PostConstruct` method. When the application stops it calls your `@PreDestroy` method. Use them to open and close resources instead of doing that work in the constructor.

example.title: The order: constructor, init, use, destroy

/spring/core/bean-lifecycle-and-scopes/s.def: A `singleton` bean (the default) is created once and shared by everyone, so it must not hold per-request state. A `prototype` bean is created fresh every time it is requested.

example.title: The same instance, or a new one each time

/spring/core/bean-lifecycle-and-scopes/l.def: By default Spring creates every singleton at startup, so mistakes show up immediately. A `@Lazy` bean is created only when it is first needed. It speeds up startup but moves any failure to run time.

example.title: When each bean is created

/spring/core/bean-lifecycle-and-scopes/b.def: A `BeanPostProcessor` is a hook that Spring calls for every bean right after it is created. It can inspect or even replace the bean. This is how Spring itself adds features such as `@Transactional` and `@Async` (by wrapping beans in proxies).

example.title: A hook that sees every bean as it is created

/spring/core/configuration-profiles-cond.def: A `@Configuration` class contains `@Bean` methods, and each method describes one bean. It is the way to register objects you do not own (such as a library class) and to wire beans together in plain Java code.

example.title: Beans that depend on each other, wired in Java

/spring/core/configuration-profiles-cond.def: A profile is a named set of beans or settings for one environment, such as `dev` or `prod`. A bean marked `@Profile("dev")` exists only when the `dev` profile is active, so one build can behave differently in each environment.

example.title: A different bean for dev and prod

/spring/core/configuration-profiles-cond.def: A conditional bean is created only when a condition is true, for example a property has a value, a class is on the classpath, or no other bean of that type exists. Spring Boot uses these conditions to decide what to auto-configure.

example.title: A feature that is switched on by a property

/spring/core/configuration-profiles-cond.def: The `Environment` is where Spring looks up settings. It reads several property sources in order (command line, environment variables, files, defaults), and the first source that has the key wins. `@Value` injects a setting, with an optional default.

example.title: Reading settings, with a default and an override

/spring/core/aop-and-proxies/around-advi.def: An `@Around` advice runs code before and after a method call and decides whether the method runs at all. It is how you add timing, logging or retries to many methods without editing them.

example.title: Timing every call of a service

/spring/core/aop-and-proxies/pointcut-ex.def: A pointcut expression says which methods an advice applies to. You can match by method signature (`execution`), by package or class (`within`), or by a custom annotation (`@annotation`). Annotations are the clearest way to mark exactly what you want.

example.title: Matching methods by a custom annotation

/spring/core/aop-and-proxies/jdk-vs-cgli.def: Spring adds behaviour by wrapping a bean in a proxy. If the bean implements an interface Spring can use a JDK proxy, which implements the same interface. Otherwise (or when forced) it subclasses the class with CGLIB. Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default.

example.title: Which kind of proxy you get

/spring/core/aop-and-proxies/self-invoca.def: Advice only runs for calls that go through the proxy. If a method calls another method of the same object with `this`, the call skips the proxy and the advice (for example `@Transactional`) does not run. Move the method to another bean to fix it.

example.title: The advice runs for the outside call only

/spring/core/application-events/publish-.def: An application event lets one part of the program announce that something happened, and other parts react without the sender knowing them. You publish an event object with `ApplicationEventPublisher` and handle it with `@EventListener`. By default the listener runs right away, in the same thread.

example.title: An order is placed, two listeners react

/spring/core/application-events/async-li.def: A normal listener runs in the publisher's thread, so a slow listener slows the publisher and an exception in it reaches the publisher. Adding `@Async` runs the listener on another thread, so the publisher continues straight away.

example.title: The listener runs on a different thread

/spring/core/application-events/transact.def: A `@TransactionalEventListener` waits until the surrounding transaction finishes. By default it runs only after a successful commit, so you never send an email for an order that was later rolled back.

example.title: The listener runs after commit, and not at all after a rollback

/spring/core/application-events/built-in.def: Spring publishes events about its own life: `ContextRefreshedEvent` when the application is ready and `ContextClosedEvent` when it shuts down. Listen to them to start work after startup or to clean up on shutdown. Spring Boot adds `ApplicationReadyEvent`.

example.title: Hooking into startup and shutdown

/spring/boot/overview/springbootapplicat.def: `@SpringBootApplication` marks the main class of a Boot app. It combines three annotations: `@Configuration` (this class defines beans), `@ComponentScan` (find beans in this package and below) and `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (set up beans from what is on the classpath).

example.title: One annotation, a working application

/spring/boot/overview/embedded-web-serve.def: A Boot web app contains its own web server (Tomcat by default). You run it like any Java program, with no separate server to install, and package it as a single executable jar.

example.title: A REST endpoint served by the built-in Tomcat

/spring/boot/overview/command-line-argum.def: Boot turns command-line arguments into settings and also gives them to your code. `--name=Asha` becomes the property `name`, and an `ApplicationRunner` can read both the options and the plain arguments after startup.

example.title: Reading options and plain arguments

/spring/boot/starters/starter-dependenci.def: A starter is one dependency that brings in everything a feature needs. `spring-boot-starter-web` adds Spring MVC, JSON support and Tomcat. You list a handful of starters instead of dozens of libraries.

example.title: Two starters in a Maven build
example.code:
<dependencies>
    <!-- web: Spring MVC, Jackson (JSON), validation hooks and the embedded Tomcat -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>

    <!-- data: Spring Data JPA, Hibernate and a connection pool -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <!-- no version numbers: the Spring Boot parent decides them -->
</dependencies>

/spring/boot/starters/boot-bom-and-versi.def: A BOM (bill of materials) is a list of library versions that are tested together. The Spring Boot parent gives you one, so you leave version numbers out and the libraries match. To change one library, set its version property.

example.title: The parent supplies versions; one property overrides one
example.code:
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.16</version>          <!-- this one number selects the whole tested set of versions -->
</parent>

<properties>
    <java.version>21</java.version>
    <!-- override one managed library, only when you must -->
    <jackson-bom.version>2.19.2</jackson-bom.version>
</properties>

/spring/boot/starters/exclude-transitive.def: A starter may bring in a library you do not want. You can exclude it, for example to replace the default Tomcat web server with Jetty. Check what you get with `mvn dependency:tree`.

example.title: Swap Tomcat for Jetty
example.code:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>                                   <!-- remove the default web server -->
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

<dependency>                                          <!-- add the one you want instead -->
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
</dependency>

/spring/boot/auto-configuration/conditio.def: Auto-configuration is a set of ordinary configuration classes guarded by conditions. `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` creates a bean only if you did not define one, so your own bean always wins. `@ConditionalOnClass` and `@ConditionalOnProperty` check the classpath and the settings.

example.title: The library default backs off when you define your own bean

/spring/boot/auto-configuration/conditio.def: When you wonder why a bean exists, or why it does not, start Boot with `--debug`. It prints a conditions report that lists every auto-configuration that matched and every one that did not, with the reason.

example.title: Finding out what Boot decided
example.code:
# print the conditions report at startup
java -jar app.jar --debug

# the report has three parts that matter:
#   Positive matches:  auto-configurations that were applied, and which condition passed
#   Negative matches:  auto-configurations that were skipped, and which condition failed
#   Unconditional classes: always applied

# on a running app with Actuator, the same information is available at:
#   GET /actuator/conditions

/spring/boot/auto-configuration/custom-a.def: You can ship auto-configuration in your own library. Write a configuration class marked `@AutoConfiguration`, make its beans conditional so users can override them, and list the class in a file under `META-INF/spring`. Boot then applies it to every app that has your jar.

example.title: An auto-configuration class and the file that registers it

/spring/boot/auto-configuration/excludin.def: If an auto-configuration gets in your way, you can turn it off with `exclude` (or the `spring.autoconfigure.exclude` property). Boot then skips it even though its conditions match.

example.title: Starting without the database setup

/spring/boot/configuration/application-y.def: Settings live outside your code in `application.yml` (or `application.properties`). YAML groups related keys by indentation and supports lists. Boot reads the file at startup, and a setting from the command line or an environment variable overrides it.

example.title: Nested settings, a list and a default
example.code:
# src/main/resources/application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: shop-service

server:
  port: 8080

shop:
  currency: INR
  free-shipping-above: 500
  allowed-countries:            # a list
    - IN
    - SG
    - AE

logging:
  level:
    com.example: DEBUG

/spring/boot/configuration/configuration.def: `@ConfigurationProperties` binds a group of related settings to one typed object, such as a record, and can validate them at startup. It is cleaner and safer than scattering `@Value` strings through the code.

example.title: Settings bound to a record, with validation

/spring/boot/configuration/profile-speci.def: A profile lets one build use different settings in each environment. Put shared settings first, then add a section (or a file such as `application-prod.yml`) for each profile and select it with `spring.profiles.active`.

example.title: Defaults plus a production override
example.code:
# application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: shop-service
server:
  port: 8080
payment:
  url: http://localhost:9000          # the default, good for local development

---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod                # only used when the "prod" profile is active
payment:
  url: https://payments.example.com
server:
  port: 80

# choose a profile at start-up:
#   java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
#   or the environment variable  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod

/spring/boot/configuration/property-prec.def: The same setting can come from several places. Boot uses a fixed order: command-line arguments beat environment variables, which beat `application.yml`, which beats defaults in code. That lets you override anything at deployment time without a rebuild.

example.title: A default is overridden from the command line

/spring/boot/actuator/health-endpoint.def: Actuator adds ready-made operational endpoints to your app. `/actuator/health` reports whether the application is up, and monitoring systems and orchestrators call it. Only the endpoints you list in `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include` are exposed.

example.title: Calling /actuator/health on a running app

/spring/boot/actuator/liveness-and-readi.def: Kubernetes asks two questions. Liveness: is the process stuck and in need of a restart? Readiness: can it take traffic right now? Boot answers both at `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`. Keep liveness simple, so a slow database never causes restarts.

example.title: The two probe endpoints

/spring/boot/actuator/custom-health-indi.def: A health indicator is a bean that reports the health of one dependency, such as a payment gateway. Return `Health.up()` or `Health.down()` with details, and Actuator adds it to `/actuator/health` automatically.

example.title: Reporting the health of a dependency

/spring/boot/actuator/micrometer-metrics.def: Micrometer is the metrics library behind Actuator. You inject a `MeterRegistry` and record counters (how many), timers (how long) and gauges (current value). Monitoring tools such as Prometheus then collect them.

example.title: Count orders and time a task

/spring/boot/actuator/exposing-endpoints.def: By default only `health` is exposed over the web. Some endpoints reveal sensitive details, such as environment values and heap dumps. Expose only what you need, secure the rest, and consider a separate management port that is not reachable from the internet.

example.title: A cautious Actuator configuration
example.code:
# application.yml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, info, metrics, prometheus     # never "*" on a public port
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized                    # hide details from anonymous callers
      probes:
        enabled: true
  server:
    port: 9090                                          # serve Actuator on a private port

/spring/boot/validation/validation-annot.def: Bean Validation lets you declare rules on fields with annotations such as `@NotBlank`, `@Email`, `@Size` and `@Min`. A validator checks an object against them and returns a list of violations.

example.title: Declaring rules and checking an object

/spring/boot/validation/valid-request-bo.def: Add `@Valid` to a `@RequestBody` parameter and Spring checks the rules before your method runs. If a rule fails, the method is not called and Spring answers with `400 Bad Request`.

example.title: An invalid request is rejected with 400

/spring/boot/validation/custom-constrain.def: When no built-in annotation fits, write your own: an annotation plus a `ConstraintValidator` class with the check. Then you can reuse the rule on any field, with a clear message.

example.title: A @StrongPassword rule

/spring/boot/validation/validation-group.def: Validation groups let the same class have different rules in different situations. For example an `id` must be empty when creating a record, but required when updating it. You name the group you want when you validate.

example.title: One class, two rule sets

/spring/boot/validation/validating-param.def: To validate simple parameters (a `@PathVariable`, a `@RequestParam` or a service method argument), put `@Validated` on the class and the constraints on the parameters. A broken rule throws a `ConstraintViolationException`.

example.title: A service that rejects bad arguments

/spring/boot/exception-handling/controll.def: A `@RestControllerAdvice` class handles exceptions for all controllers in one place. Each `@ExceptionHandler` method turns one kind of exception into an HTTP status and a response body, so controllers stay clean and every error looks the same.

example.title: Turning a NotFound exception into a 404

/spring/boot/exception-handling/problemd.def: `ProblemDetail` (RFC 9457, in Spring 6) is a standard shape for error responses: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`. Using it means every client sees the same, predictable error format.

example.title: A standard JSON error body
