/spring/boot/exception-handling/response.def: For a quick one-off error you can throw `ResponseStatusException` with a status and a reason from the controller. Spring turns it into that response, without writing a handler or a custom exception class.

example.title: Throwing a status from a controller

/spring/boot/testing-basics/junit5-and-a.def: A unit test is a small method marked `@Test` that runs one piece of code and checks the result. JUnit 5 finds and runs the tests, and AssertJ gives readable assertions such as `assertThat(x).isEqualTo(y)`.

example.title: Two tests for a small class

/spring/boot/testing-basics/mockito-mock.def: A mock is a stand-in for a dependency, such as a repository or a payment client, so a test can run without a database or network. You tell the mock what to return with `when(...)`, and afterwards check how it was used with `verify(...)`.

example.title: Testing a service with a mocked repository

/spring/boot/testing-basics/parameterize.def: A parameterized test runs the same test body with many inputs, so one method covers many cases. Each row of `@CsvSource` becomes its own test run.

example.title: One test, four inputs

/spring/boot/testing-basics/testing-exce.def: Use `assertThrows` to check that bad input fails the right way. `@BeforeEach` runs before every test and gives each one a fresh object, so tests never depend on each other.

example.title: A fresh account for each test

/spring/boot/testing-slices-testcontaine.def: `@WebMvcTest` starts only the web layer (controllers, JSON, validation), not the whole application, so it is fast. You send fake HTTP requests with `MockMvc` and replace the services with mocks.

example.title: Testing a controller on its own

/spring/boot/testing-slices-testcontaine.def: `@DataJpaTest` starts only the JPA layer: entities, repositories and an in-memory database. Each test runs in a transaction that is rolled back afterwards, so tests stay isolated.

example.title: Testing a repository against an in-memory database

/spring/boot/testing-slices-testcontaine.def: `@SpringBootTest` starts the whole application context, so you can test the real wiring from controller to database. It is the slowest kind of test, so keep it for a few end-to-end checks.

example.title: The full application, called over MockMvc

/spring/boot/testing-slices-testcontaine.def: Testcontainers starts a real database (or Kafka, Redis and more) in a Docker container for the duration of a test. Tests then run against the same engine as production, not a lookalike such as H2.

example.title: A repository test against real PostgreSQL

/spring/data/jpa-basics/entities-and-ids.def: An entity is a plain class mapped to a database table. `@Entity` marks it, `@Id` marks the primary key, and `@GeneratedValue` lets the database or Hibernate create the id. A repository saves and loads entities without any SQL.

example.title: Save an entity and read it back

/spring/data/jpa-basics/derived-queries.def: Spring Data builds queries from method names. `findByCityAndAgeGreaterThan` becomes a `WHERE` clause with no code from you. You can also use `existsBy`, `countBy` and `OrderBy`.

example.title: Queries written as method names

/spring/data/jpa-basics/query-annotation.def: When a method name would get too long, write the query yourself with `@Query`. JPQL talks about entities and fields instead of tables and columns, and `@Param` binds the named parameters safely.

example.title: A custom query with a named parameter

/spring/data/jpa-basics/relationships.def: Entities relate like tables do. `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToOne` model a parent with many children, `mappedBy` says which side owns the foreign key, and `cascade` saves the children together with the parent.

example.title: An author with books, saved in one call

/spring/data/jpa-basics/pagination-and-s.def: Never load a whole table to show one page. Pass a `Pageable` to a repository method and Spring Data adds `LIMIT`, `OFFSET` and `ORDER BY`. The returned `Page` also knows the total number of rows and pages.

example.title: The second page of three items, newest first

/spring/data/n-plus-one-lazy-loading/wha.def: The N+1 problem is one query to load a list, plus one extra query for each item when you touch its lazy relationship. With 100 authors that is 101 queries instead of 1. It is invisible in the code and slow in production.

example.title: Counting the queries behind a simple loop

/spring/data/n-plus-one-lazy-loading/joi.def: `JOIN FETCH` tells JPA to load the parent and its children in the same query. The loop then reads data that is already in memory and the extra queries disappear.

example.title: One query instead of four

/spring/data/n-plus-one-lazy-loading/ent.def: `@EntityGraph` does the same job as `JOIN FETCH` without writing JPQL. You name the relationships to load eagerly for that one repository method and keep the rest lazy.

example.title: Load books together with authors on one method

/spring/data/n-plus-one-lazy-loading/bat.def: `@BatchSize` loads the lazy collections of many parents in one query using `IN (...)`. It turns N+1 into 1+1 and is handy when a join would repeat a lot of data.

example.title: Two queries however many authors there are

/spring/data/n-plus-one-lazy-loading/dto.def: If a screen only needs a few columns, do not load whole entities. A projection selects exactly those columns into a small record, which also removes lazy-loading surprises.

example.title: Select only what the screen shows

/spring/data/sql-tuning-indexing/reading.def: `EXPLAIN` shows how the database will run a query. A table scan reads every row, while an index lookup jumps straight to the matching rows. Check the plan first, before you guess what is slow.

example.title: The same query before and after adding an index

/spring/data/sql-tuning-indexing/composi.def: A composite index covers several columns, and the order matters. Put the columns you compare with `=` first and the range column (`>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`) last, so one index serves the whole `WHERE`.

example.title: One index for an equality plus a range

/spring/data/sql-tuning-indexing/functio.def: Wrapping an indexed column in a function, such as `UPPER(email)`, stops the database from using the index normally. Compare the column to a plain value, or create an index on the expression itself.

example.title: A plain comparison against a function call

/spring/data/sql-tuning-indexing/like-an.def: An index is sorted, so it can answer a prefix search such as `LIKE abc%` by jumping to where abc starts. A leading wildcard, as in `LIKE %abc`, gives no starting point and forces a full scan. For that kind of search use a full-text index.

example.title: A prefix search against a suffix search

/spring/data/caching/cacheable-basics.def: Put `@Cacheable` on a method and Spring remembers its result for each argument. The next call with the same argument returns the stored value and the method body does not run. Turn caching on with `@EnableCaching`.

example.title: The second call never reaches the method

/spring/data/caching/cache-evict-and-put.def: A cache must change when the data changes. `@CacheEvict` removes the stale entry after an update, and `@CachePut` replaces it with the new value so the next read is already fresh.

example.title: Updating a value and clearing the old copy

/spring/data/caching/cache-keys-and-cond.def: The cache key defaults to the method arguments, and `key` lets you choose it with an expression. `condition` decides whether to use the cache for a call, and `unless` decides whether to store a result, for example never store `null`.

example.title: Choosing the key and skipping empty results

/spring/data/caching/caffeine-expiry.def: The default cache never forgets. Caffeine is a fast in-memory cache that adds a size limit and expiry, so old entries disappear on their own. Boot configures it from the `spring.cache.caffeine.spec` setting.

example.title: An entry that expires after one second

/spring/data/transactions/transactional-.def: A transaction makes several database changes succeed or fail together. Put `@Transactional` on a service method: if it finishes normally Spring commits, and if it throws a runtime exception Spring rolls everything back.

example.title: A failed transfer leaves both balances untouched

/spring/data/transactions/rollback-rules.def: By default Spring rolls back only for runtime exceptions and errors. A checked exception still commits the work done so far. Add `rollbackFor = Exception.class` when a checked exception should undo the changes too.

example.title: A checked exception commits unless you say otherwise

/spring/data/transactions/propagation.def: Propagation says what happens when a transactional method calls another one. The default, `REQUIRED`, joins the transaction of the caller. `REQUIRES_NEW` starts a separate one, so for example an audit record survives even if the caller rolls back.

example.title: The audit row stays, the order row does not

/spring/data/transactions/self-invocatio.def: `@Transactional` works through a proxy around the bean. A method that calls another method of the same class skips the proxy, so the annotation on the inner method is ignored. Call it from another bean, or split the class.

example.title: The same failing code, with and without the proxy

/spring/data/transactions/programmatic-t.def: `TransactionTemplate` gives you the same transaction in plain code. It is useful when only part of a method needs a transaction, or when you want to decide yourself when to roll back.

example.title: Rolling back by hand

/spring/data/locking/optimistic-locking.def: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare. A `@Version` column counts the changes to a row. When two users edit the same row, the second save finds the version has moved on and fails instead of silently overwriting the first change.

example.title: The second, stale update is rejected

/spring/data/locking/retry-on-conflict.def: An optimistic-lock failure is not a bug: someone else changed the row first. The usual answer is to reload the fresh data and try again a few times, then give up with a clear error.

example.title: A conflict on the first attempt, success on the second

/spring/data/locking/pessimistic-locking.def: Pessimistic locking takes a lock on the row when you read it, using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, so nobody else can change it until your transaction ends. Use it when conflicts are common and a retry would be costly.

example.title: Reading a row with a write lock

/spring/security/security-architecture/f.def: Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters that every request passes through before it reaches your controller. You describe the chain in a `SecurityFilterChain` bean: which URLs are open, which need a login, and how the user proves who they are.

example.title: Public, protected and authenticated requests

/spring/security/security-architecture/a.def: Authentication answers "who are you?" and authorization answers "what may you do?". Rules such as `hasRole("ADMIN")` on a URL pattern let the filter chain refuse a logged-in user with `403 Forbidden` when the role is missing.

example.title: An admin-only URL

/spring/security/security-architecture/p.def: Never store passwords as plain text. A `PasswordEncoder` such as BCrypt stores a salted, slow hash. The same password gives a different hash each time, and `matches` checks a login attempt against the stored value.

example.title: Hash a password and check it

/spring/security/security-architecture/u.def: Spring Security loads users through a `UserDetailsService`, usually from your database. An `AuthenticationProvider` then compares the password with the stored hash and, on success, returns an `Authentication` that holds the user and their authorities.

example.title: Logging a user in against a custom user store

/spring/security/security-architecture/c.def: CSRF tricks a logged-in browser into sending a request you did not intend. Spring Security blocks state-changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE) that lack a CSRF token. APIs that use tokens in headers instead of cookies can switch it off for their own paths.

example.title: A POST without a token is blocked

/spring/security/jwt/jwt-structure.def: A JSON Web Token is three Base64URL parts joined by dots: a header (the algorithm), a payload of claims (who the user is and when the token expires) and a signature. The payload is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read it.

example.title: Build a token and read its parts

/spring/security/jwt/signing-and-verifyi.def: The signature proves the token was issued by someone who knows the secret and has not been changed. The server recomputes the signature on every request. Edit one character of the payload and the check fails.

example.title: A tampered token is detected

/spring/security/jwt/jwt-encoder-decoder.def: Spring Security ships a `JwtEncoder` to create tokens and a `JwtDecoder` to verify them. The decoder checks the signature and the expiry date for you, and throws an exception when either is wrong.

example.title: Issue a token, then read it back

/spring/security/jwt/resource-server-jwt.def: An API that accepts JWTs is an OAuth2 resource server. Configure `oauth2ResourceServer(jwt)` with a `JwtDecoder` and every request must carry `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Spring validates it and gives your controller the `Jwt`.

example.title: Calls with no token, a bad token and a good token

/spring/security/oauth2-oidc/authorizati.def: OAuth2 lets a user give your app limited access without sharing a password. The app sends the user to the login server, gets back a short-lived code, and exchanges that code for tokens. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds an ID token that says who the user is.

example.title: The two requests behind "Log in with ..."
example.code:
# 1. The browser is redirected to the authorization server
GET https://auth.example.com/authorize
      ?response_type=code
      &client_id=shop-web
      &redirect_uri=https://shop.example.com/login/callback
      &scope=openid profile email        # "openid" turns on OIDC and the ID token
      &state=af0ifjsldkj                 # a random value, checked on return to stop forged callbacks

# 2. After the user logs in, the browser returns to the redirect_uri with ?code=...&state=...
#    The backend of the app then swaps the code for tokens (never done in the browser)
curl -X POST https://auth.example.com/token \
     -d grant_type=authorization_code \
     -d code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA \
     -d redirect_uri=https://shop.example.com/login/callback \
     -d client_id=shop-web \
     -d client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET

# response: { "access_token": "...", "id_token": "...", "refresh_token": "...", "expires_in": 300 }

/spring/security/oauth2-oidc/pkce.def: PKCE protects the code flow for apps that cannot keep a secret, such as single-page and mobile apps. The app invents a random `code_verifier`, sends only its SHA-256 hash (the `code_challenge`) first, and proves it owns the verifier when exchanging the code.

example.title: Computing the code challenge

/spring/security/oauth2-oidc/scopes-to-a.def: A token carries scopes such as `read` or `write`. Spring turns them into authorities (`SCOPE_read`) that your rules can check with `hasAuthority`. You can change the claim name and the prefix when your provider puts roles somewhere else.

example.title: Mapping token claims to authorities

/spring/security/oauth2-oidc/resource-se.def: In production the tokens come from an identity provider such as Keycloak, Okta or Auth0. Give the resource server its `issuer-uri` and Spring downloads the public keys of the provider, checks the signature, and validates the issuer and expiry for every request.

example.title: Resource server configuration
example.code:
# application.yml
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com/realms/shop     # keys are found at <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration
          # audiences: shop-api                                  # optionally require a matching aud claim

/spring/security/method-security/preauth.def: Method security puts the rule next to the code it protects, so it holds whether the method is called from a controller, a scheduler or a message listener. `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` runs the check before the method body, and refuses with `AccessDeniedException`.

example.title: Only admins may call the method

/spring/security/method-security/preauth.def: The expression can use the method arguments and the logged-in user. `#owner == authentication.name` lets users read their own data, and `or hasRole('ADMIN')` lets admins read anyone's.

example.title: Users see only their own orders

/spring/security/method-security/postaut.def: `@PostAuthorize` runs after the method and can look at what it returned. It suits cases where you only know who owns the data once you have loaded it, such as a document fetched by id.

example.title: Check the owner of the loaded document

/spring/security/method-security/postfil.def: `@PostFilter` removes the items of a returned list that the user may not see. It is convenient for small lists. For large tables, filter in the database query instead, so you do not load rows you will throw away.

example.title: A list reduced to the caller's own notes

/spring/security/common-vulnerabilities/.def: SQL injection happens when user input is glued into a query string, so the input can change the meaning of the query. Parameterized queries send the input as data, never as SQL, which makes the attack impossible.

example.title: The same input against an unsafe and a safe query

/spring/security/common-vulnerabilities/.def: XSS means the app shows user input in a page without escaping it, so the browser runs the script of the attacker. Escape every user-supplied value for the place it is written (HTML, attribute, JavaScript or URL). Template engines such as Thymeleaf do this by default.

example.title: Escaping before writing to HTML

/spring/security/common-vulnerabilities/.def: Being logged in is not the same as being allowed. If `/invoices/42` returns invoice 42 to anyone with a login, users can walk through the data of other people by changing the number. Always check that the object belongs to the caller.

example.title: An ownership check on every lookup

/spring/security/common-vulnerabilities/.def: Response headers tell the browser how careful to be. Spring Security adds several by default, such as `X-Content-Type-Options` and `X-Frame-Options` (against clickjacking). You can add more, such as a Content-Security-Policy that limits where scripts may load from.

example.title: Default headers plus a Content-Security-Policy

/microservices/overview/own-your-data.def: In a microservice system each service keeps its own database, and other services can only reach that data through its API. This keeps services independent: one team can change its tables without breaking anyone else.

example.title: The order service asks the customer service, never its database

/microservices/overview/bounded-context.def: The same word means different things in different parts of a business. A customer in billing has a credit limit, and a customer in shipping has a delivery address. Each service models only what its own context needs and shares just the id.

example.title: Two models of a customer

/microservices/overview/independent-depl.def: Each service is built, tested and released on its own, in its own container, with its own database. A change to the orders service can go to production without redeploying payments.

example.title: Two services, two databases, one compose file
example.code:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  orders:
    image: shop/orders:1.4.2            # released on its own schedule
    ports: ["8081:8080"]
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://orders-db:5432/orders
    depends_on: [orders-db]

  orders-db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine           # owned by orders only

  payments:
    image: shop/payments:2.0.0          # a different version, a different team
    ports: ["8082:8080"]
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://payments-db:5432/payments
    depends_on: [payments-db]

  payments-db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine

/microservices/overview/strangler-fig.def: To move from a monolith, do not rewrite everything at once. Put a router in front, and move one feature at a time to a new service. The router sends migrated paths to the new service and everything else to the old monolith, until the monolith is empty.

example.title: A router that moves traffic path by path

/microservices/infrastructure/api-gatewa.def: A gateway maps the public URL to the internal service that handles it. With Spring Cloud Gateway each route has an id, a target `uri`, and predicates (conditions such as the path) that decide which requests it takes.

example.title: Two routes in application.yml
example.code:
# application.yml (Spring Cloud Gateway)
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: orders
          uri: lb://orders-service              # lb:// = look the instances up in service discovery
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/orders/**
        - id: payments
          uri: http://payments:8080
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/payments/**
            - Method=GET,POST

/microservices/infrastructure/api-gatewa.def: Filters change a request on its way in and the response on its way out. Common ones strip a path prefix, add a header, retry a failed call or limit the request rate, so these jobs do not have to be repeated in every service.

example.title: Filters on one route
example.code:
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: orders
          uri: lb://orders-service
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/orders/**
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=1                      # /api/orders/7  ->  /orders/7
            - AddRequestHeader=X-Source, gateway
            - name: Retry
              args:
                retries: 2
                statuses: BAD_GATEWAY
            - name: RequestRateLimiter           # needs Redis to share counters between gateway instances
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20

/microservices/infrastructure/api-gatewa.def: A token bucket allows a short burst but limits the long-run rate. The bucket holds a fixed number of tokens, each request takes one, and tokens are added back at a steady speed. An empty bucket means `429 Too Many Requests`.

example.title: Three requests pass, the fourth waits

/microservices/infrastructure/api-gatewa.def: The gateway can check the token once, reject bad requests early, and pass the user identity to the services in a header. The internal services then trust the gateway instead of each parsing the token again, as long as they are not reachable from outside.

example.title: Check the token, forward the user id

/microservices/infrastructure/service-di.def: Instances register themselves with the registry when they start and send a heartbeat every few seconds. If the heartbeats stop, the registry removes the instance after a timeout, so callers are never sent to a dead server.

example.title: An instance that stops sending heartbeats disappears

/microservices/infrastructure/service-di.def: With client-side load balancing the caller asks the registry for the list of instances and picks one itself, for example in turn (round robin). No separate load balancer sits in the path, and Spring Cloud LoadBalancer does this behind `lb://service-name`.

example.title: Round robin over discovered instances

/microservices/infrastructure/service-di.def: Eureka is a registry from Netflix, packaged in Spring Cloud. A service adds the Eureka client dependency and the registry address, and it registers and sends heartbeats on its own.

example.title: Client configuration
example.code:
# application.yml of the orders service
spring:
  application:
    name: orders-service                  # the name other services use: lb://orders-service

eureka:
  client:
    service-url:
      defaultZone: http://eureka:8761/eureka
  instance:
    prefer-ip-address: true
    lease-renewal-interval-in-seconds: 10     # heartbeat every 10 s
    lease-expiration-duration-in-seconds: 30  # removed after 30 s of silence

/microservices/infrastructure/service-di.def: On Kubernetes you often need no registry at all. A `Service` gives a set of pods one stable DNS name, and Kubernetes keeps its list of healthy pods up to date. Callers simply use `http://orders`.

example.title: A Service and the URL that uses it
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders                  # becomes the DNS name  http://orders  (or orders.<namespace>.svc)
spec:
  selector:
    app: orders                 # every ready pod with this label is behind the name
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

# in another service:
#   RestClient.create("http://orders").get().uri("/orders/7")...

/microservices/infrastructure/config-ser.def: A config server is a small Spring Boot app marked `@EnableConfigServer` that reads settings from a Git repository and serves them over HTTP. Changing a setting then means a Git commit, with history and review, instead of editing servers.

example.title: The server and where it reads from
example.code:
# the application class carries the annotation:
#   @SpringBootApplication
#   @EnableConfigServer
#   public class ConfigServerApplication { ... }

# application.yml of the config server
server:
  port: 8888
spring:
  cloud:
    config:
      server:
        git:
          uri: https://github.com/example/shop-config    # one repository for all services
          default-label: main
          search-paths: "{application}"                   # a folder per service

/microservices/infrastructure/config-ser.def: A service names the config server with `spring.config.import`, and its settings are fetched at startup, before the beans are created. The service name and active profile decide which files are used.

example.title: A client that imports its settings
example.code:
# application.yml of the orders service
spring:
  application:
    name: orders-service                                   # looks for orders-service.yml in the config repository
  profiles:
    active: prod                                           # ... and orders-service-prod.yml
  config:
    import: "optional:configserver:http://config-server:8888"   # "optional:" lets the service start if the server is down

/microservices/infrastructure/config-ser.def: The repository holds a shared file for all services, a file per service, and a file per service and profile. More specific files win, so a production value overrides the default one.

example.title: The layout in the Git repository
example.code:
# shop-config/                    (the Git repository)
#   application.yml               shared by every service
#   orders-service.yml            only for orders-service
#   orders-service-prod.yml       orders-service when the "prod" profile is active

# application.yml
logging:
  level:
    root: INFO

# orders-service.yml
orders:
  max-items-per-order: 20

# orders-service-prod.yml            (wins over the file above in production)
orders:
  max-items-per-order: 50

/microservices/infrastructure/config-ser.def: Beans marked `@RefreshScope` are rebuilt when the application receives a refresh signal, so they read the new values from the config server. You trigger it with a call to the Actuator `refresh` endpoint, or let a bus broadcast it to every instance.

example.title: Refreshing one instance
example.code:
# 1. commit the new value to the config repository
git commit -am "raise max items per order" && git push

# 2. tell a running instance to re-read its configuration
curl -X POST http://orders:8080/actuator/refresh
# ["orders.max-items-per-order"]        <- the names of the properties that changed

# it needs the endpoint exposed:  management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=refresh
# and beans that should change at runtime annotated with  @RefreshScope

/microservices/communication/service-com.def: The most common way for one service to call another is a synchronous HTTP request. Spring's `RestClient` gives a short, fluent API: set a base URL once, then build requests and read the body as a type.

example.title: The order service reads a price from the catalog service

/microservices/communication/service-com.def: A remote call without a timeout can wait forever and tie up a thread, and enough stuck threads bring your service down too. Set a connect timeout and a read timeout on every client, and choose values shorter than your own caller's timeout.

example.title: A slow service is cut off after 300 ms

/microservices/communication/service-com.def: With messaging the caller does not wait. It drops an event on a queue and carries on, and a consumer handles it later at its own pace. The two services are decoupled in time, and a slow or restarting consumer does not slow the producer.

example.title: The order is accepted at once, processed later

/microservices/communication/service-com.def: gRPC calls a remote method as if it were a local one, using a binary format that is smaller and faster than JSON. The `.proto` file is the contract: both sides generate their client and server code from it, so a mismatch is caught at build time.

example.title: A service contract in Protocol Buffers

/microservices/resilience/resilience4j/r.def: Retry calls the operation again after a failure, which fixes short glitches such as a dropped connection. Limit the number of attempts, wait between them, and only retry things that are safe to repeat.

example.title: A call that succeeds on the third try

/microservices/resilience/resilience4j/c.def: A circuit breaker stops calling a service that keeps failing. After too many failures it opens and rejects calls immediately, giving the service time to recover and keeping your threads free. After a wait it lets a few calls through to test the water.

example.title: The breaker opens after repeated failures

/microservices/resilience/resilience4j/b.def: A bulkhead limits how many calls to one dependency run at the same time, like the watertight compartments of a ship. If that dependency becomes slow, only its own share of threads is used up, and the rest of the service keeps working.

example.title: Only two concurrent calls are allowed

/microservices/resilience/resilience4j/t.def: A time limiter stops waiting for an asynchronous call after a deadline and fails with a timeout. It keeps one slow dependency from holding up your whole request.

example.title: Waiting at most 200 ms for a slow future

/microservices/resilience/resilience4j/r.def: A rate limiter caps how many calls are made per period, to protect a dependency with a quota. A fallback gives the caller a sensible answer when the call fails or is refused, such as cached data, so one failure does not become an error page.

example.title: A fallback answer when the limit is reached

/microservices/data-consistency/saga/orc.def: In an orchestrated saga one coordinator calls the steps in order: reserve stock, take payment, ship. If a step fails, it runs the undo actions of the steps that already succeeded. The flow is easy to read in one place.

example.title: A coordinator that runs steps and undoes them on failure

/microservices/data-consistency/saga/com.def: A saga cannot roll back like a database transaction, because each step has already been committed. Instead every step has a compensating action that undoes its business effect: release the reservation, refund the payment. Compensations must be safe to run more than once.

example.title: Undoing a reservation, safely twice

/microservices/data-consistency/saga/cho.def: In a choreographed saga there is no coordinator. Each service listens for events and reacts: stock is reserved, so payment starts; payment fails, so stock is released. It is loosely coupled, but the overall flow is spread across the services and harder to follow.

example.title: Services reacting to events

/microservices/data-consistency/outbox-i.def: Saving to the database and publishing an event are two systems, so one can succeed while the other fails. The outbox pattern writes the event to an `outbox` table in the same database transaction as the change. Both are saved, or neither is.

example.title: The order and its event commit together or not at all

/microservices/data-consistency/outbox-i.def: A separate relay process reads the unsent rows from the outbox, publishes them to the broker, and marks them as sent. If it crashes between publishing and marking, the event is published again, so delivery is at least once and consumers must cope with duplicates.

example.title: A crash after publishing causes a duplicate

/microservices/data-consistency/outbox-i.def: An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. The client sends a unique idempotency key with a payment request. The server remembers the key and its result, and returns the stored answer instead of charging again on a retry.

example.title: A retried payment is charged once

/microservices/data-consistency/outbox-i.def: Because brokers deliver at least once, a consumer must be ready for the same message twice. It records the ids of the messages it has handled, in the same transaction as the effect, and skips any id it has seen.

example.title: A duplicate message is ignored

/microservices/data-consistency/cqrs-eve.def: CQRS (command query responsibility segregation) uses one model to change data and another, shaped for screens, to read it. The write side enforces the rules. The read side is a simple, fast copy, such as a table with the totals already added up.

example.title: Commands change the write model, queries read a summary

/microservices/data-consistency/cqrs-eve.def: Event sourcing stores every change as an event, never the current state. The current state is worked out by replaying the events from the start. You get a full audit trail for free and can rebuild the state as it was at any moment.

example.title: The balance is the sum of the events

/microservices/data-consistency/cqrs-eve.def: Replaying thousands of events for every request gets slow. A snapshot saves the state at a certain event number. To load the aggregate you take the latest snapshot and replay only the events after it.

example.title: Start from a snapshot instead of event 1

/microservices/data-consistency/cqrs-eve.def: When the read model is updated by a separate process, a query right after a command may still show the old data for a moment. The two models become consistent soon after. Design the screens for it, for example by showing the result of the command directly.

example.title: A read right after a write is briefly stale

/microservices/observability/observabili.def: For every service, measure three things: Rate (requests per second), Errors (how many fail) and Duration (how long they take). Together they tell you whether users are being served well. Micrometer collects them with a counter and a timer.

example.title: Count requests and errors, time the calls

/microservices/observability/observabili.def: One user request passes through many services. A correlation id is a unique value created at the edge and passed along in a header. Every service puts it in its log lines (through the logging MDC), so you can find all the lines of one request.

example.title: A filter that stores the id for the whole request

/microservices/observability/observabili.def: Distributed tracing joins the work of many services into one trace. The `traceparent` header (W3C standard) carries the trace id and the id of the calling span. Each service creates a new span with the same trace id and forwards the header to the next one.

example.title: Passing a trace to the next service

/microservices/observability/observabili.def: A service level objective (SLO) is a target such as 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. The gap to 100% is the error budget: the amount of failure you can afford. While budget remains you can ship fast, and when it runs out you slow down and fix reliability.

example.title: How much downtime does 99.9% allow?

/databases/relational-design/normalizati.def: Normalization means storing each fact in one place. If a customer's city is copied onto every order row, changing it means updating many rows, and missing one leaves the data inconsistent. Split the data into tables and join them when you read.

example.title: Customers and orders in separate tables

/databases/relational-design/constraints.def: Constraints are rules the database enforces for you: `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY` and `CHECK`. Bad data is rejected at the door, whichever application or script tries to write it.

example.title: Four kinds of bad data, four rejections

/databases/relational-design/many-to-man.def: A student takes many courses and a course has many students. A relational table cannot hold a list, so a third table, a junction table, holds one row per pair. Its primary key is the pair of ids, which also prevents duplicates.

example.title: A junction table between students and courses

/databases/relational-design/surrogate-a.def: A natural key is a value from the real world, such as an email or an ISBN. A surrogate key is a meaningless generated number. Use a surrogate id as the primary key, since real-world values change, and keep the natural key with a `UNIQUE` constraint.

example.title: A generated id plus a unique business key

/databases/sql-patterns/joins.def: An inner join keeps only the rows that match on both sides. A left join keeps every row from the left table and fills the missing right-hand columns with `NULL`, which is how you list customers even when they have no orders.

example.title: Customers with and without orders

/databases/sql-patterns/anti-join.def: To find rows that have no related row, such as customers who never ordered, use `NOT EXISTS`. It is clear, fast, and safe with `NULL`s. `NOT IN` is a trap: if the subquery returns even one `NULL`, it matches nothing at all.

example.title: Customers who have never ordered

/databases/sql-patterns/group-by-having.def: `GROUP BY` collapses rows into one row per group so you can count and add up. `WHERE` filters rows before grouping, and `HAVING` filters the groups afterwards, for example only customers who spent more than 150.

example.title: Total spend per customer, big spenders only

/databases/sql-patterns/window-functions.def: A window function calculates across a set of related rows without collapsing them, as `GROUP BY` does. Use it for rankings, running totals and the previous row's value, with `OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)`.

example.title: Rank and running total per customer
example.code:
CREATE TABLE sales (customer VARCHAR(10), sale_day INT, amount INT);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES ('asha', 1, 100), ('asha', 2, 50), ('asha', 3, 200), ('ravi', 1, 70), ('ravi', 2, 30);

-- columns: customer, sale_day, amount, rank of the amount, running total
SELECT customer, sale_day, amount,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY amount DESC) AS amount_rank,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY sale_day) AS running_total
FROM sales
ORDER BY customer, sale_day;

-- Output:
-- asha | 1 | 100 | 2 | 100
-- asha | 2 | 50 | 3 | 150
-- asha | 3 | 200 | 1 | 350
-- ravi | 1 | 70 | 1 | 70
-- ravi | 2 | 30 | 2 | 100

/databases/sql-patterns/recursive-cte.def: A common table expression (CTE) names a sub-query. A recursive one refers to itself, which is how you walk a hierarchy of unknown depth, such as an organisation chart: start from the top and keep adding the people who report to the last level.

example.title: Everyone under the CEO, with their level
example.code:
CREATE TABLE staff (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10), manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO staff VALUES (1, 'Meera', NULL), (2, 'Asha', 1), (3, 'Ravi', 1), (4, 'Kiran', 2), (5, 'Dev', 4);

-- columns: name, level below the CEO
WITH RECURSIVE chain(id, name, level) AS (
    SELECT id, name, 0 FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL         -- the starting point
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, c.level + 1
    FROM staff s JOIN chain c ON s.manager_id = c.id                -- add the next level
)
SELECT name, level FROM chain ORDER BY level, name;

-- Output:
-- Meera | 0
-- Asha | 1
-- Ravi | 1
-- Kiran | 2
-- Dev | 3

/databases/sql-patterns/upsert-merge.def: An upsert inserts a row if it is new and updates it if it exists, in one atomic statement. That avoids the race in "select, then insert or update". The standard form is `MERGE`, and PostgreSQL also offers `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`.

example.title: Insert new products, update existing ones

/databases/sql-patterns/keyset-paginatio.def: `OFFSET 100000` makes the database read and throw away 100,000 rows before returning the page, so deep pages are slow. Keyset pagination remembers the last id seen and asks for the rows after it, which uses the index and stays fast on every page.

example.title: The next page starts after the last id

/databases/schema-migrations/flyway-vers.def: Flyway applies numbered SQL scripts (`V1__...`, `V2__...`) in order, once each, and records them in a history table. Every environment ends up with the same schema, and a new developer or server only gets the scripts it has not run yet.

example.title: Two scripts applied, a second run does nothing

/databases/schema-migrations/flyway-chec.def: Flyway stores a checksum of every script it has run. If you edit an old script, the checksum no longer matches and validation fails, because other databases already ran the old version. Fix mistakes with a new migration instead.

example.title: An edited script is detected

/databases/schema-migrations/expand-and-.def: To change a column without downtime, do it in small steps that each work with both the old and the new code. Expand: add the new column and copy the data. Switch the application over. Contract: drop the old column in a later release.

example.title: Renaming a column in three safe steps

/databases/schema-migrations/baseline-ex.def: A database that already exists has no history table. A baseline tells Flyway "everything up to version 1 is already here", so it skips the scripts up to the baseline and applies only the newer ones.

example.title: Baseline at version 1, then migrate

/databases/acid-isolation-mvcc/atomicity.def: Atomic means a transaction is all or nothing. If anything fails halfway, the database undoes every change made so far, so you never see a transfer where the money left one account but did not reach the other.

example.title: A failed transfer is rolled back

/databases/acid-isolation-mvcc/read-comm.def: Isolation decides what one transaction can see of another one's changes. Under `READ COMMITTED` a second read of the same row can return a new value (a non-repeatable read). Under `REPEATABLE READ` the transaction keeps seeing the data as it was when it started.

example.title: The same read twice, under two isolation levels

/databases/acid-isolation-mvcc/lost-upda.def: A lost update happens when two transactions read the same value, each compute a new one, and the last write silently erases the first. Avoid it by doing the arithmetic inside the `UPDATE` statement, or by locking or versioning the row.

example.title: Read-modify-write against an atomic update

/databases/acid-isolation-mvcc/mvcc-read.def: With multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) the database keeps old versions of changed rows. A reader sees the last committed version while a writer is still working, so reads do not wait for writes and writes do not wait for reads.

example.title: A reader is not blocked by an open write

/databases/acid-isolation-mvcc/row-locki.def: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the rows it returns until the transaction ends. A second transaction asking for the same rows must wait, and fails with a timeout if the lock is not released. It is how you safely read-then-change a row that many users compete for.

example.title: The second transaction cannot take the lock

/databases/replication-sharding/read-rep.def: A primary database takes the writes and copies them to read replicas, which serve reads and spread the load. The copy is not instant: for a short time a replica is behind (replication lag), so a read right after a write may return old data.

example.title: A stale read from a replica

/databases/replication-sharding/hash-sha.def: Sharding splits the rows of one table across several database servers. A common rule is `hash(key) % number_of_shards`. It spreads the data evenly, but if you add a shard the modulus changes and most keys move to a different server.

example.title: How many keys move when a fourth shard is added

/databases/replication-sharding/consiste.def: Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring. A key belongs to the next server clockwise. When a server is added, it only takes over the keys between itself and its neighbour, so only about 1/N of the keys move instead of most of them.

example.title: Adding a fourth node moves far fewer keys

/databases/replication-sharding/table-pa.def: Partitioning splits one big table into smaller physical pieces inside one database, usually by date. Queries on a date range read only the matching partitions, and old data can be removed by dropping a whole partition, which is instant.

example.title: Monthly range partitions in PostgreSQL

/databases/nosql-and-redis/cache-aside.def: In cache-aside the application looks in the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache and returns it. When the data changes it deletes the cached copy. Redis is the usual cache, and the logic is the same with any store.

example.title: Read through the cache, invalidate on update

/databases/nosql-and-redis/redis-strings.def: The simplest Redis type is a string stored under a key. `SET` and `GET` store and read it, `EXPIRE` makes it disappear after some seconds, and `INCR` adds one atomically, so it is safe as a counter or rate limiter even with many clients.

example.title: A short redis-cli session
example.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET session:42 "asha"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> EXPIRE session:42 30        # forget it after 30 seconds
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> GET session:42
"asha"

127.0.0.1:6379> INCR visits:home            # atomic, even with thousands of clients
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR visits:home
(integer) 2

/databases/nosql-and-redis/redis-sorted-.def: A sorted set keeps unique members ordered by a score. Adding, updating a score and reading the top N are all fast, which makes it a natural fit for leaderboards and priority queues.

example.title: A leaderboard
example.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD leaderboard 250 asha 300 ravi 180 mei
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> ZINCRBY leaderboard 100 mei      # mei scores again: 180 + 100
"280"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 1 WITHSCORES      # the top two
1) "ravi"
2) "300"
3) "mei"
4) "280"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZREVRANK leaderboard asha      # position counted from the top, starting at 0
(integer) 2

/databases/nosql-and-redis/document-mode.def: A document database such as MongoDB stores each record as a JSON-like document. Related data that is read together, such as an order and its items, lives inside one document, so one read returns everything. The cost is that the data is repeated and joins are limited.

example.title: An order with its items embedded
